Four trials with 189 eyes assessed the effect of anti-VEGF for preexisting maculopathy, and three trials with 110 eyes compared different anti-VEGF treatment modalities. In the preventive anti-VEGF treatment meta-analysis over a 24-month follow-up, the anti-VEGF group exhibited significantly fewer cases of radiation maculopathy (odds ratio: 0.40; 95% confidence interval: 0.25, 0.66, P = 0.0003, I 2 = 45%). For the meta-analysis of anti-VEGF treatment for preexisting radiation maculopathy over a 6-month follow-up, the anti-VEGF group showed improved visual acuity (SMD: -1.13, 95% confidence interval, -1.69 to -0.56, P < 0.0000, I 2 = 47%) and decreased central macular thickness (SMD: -0.59, 95% confidence interval, -1.13 to -0.05, P = 0.03, I 2 = 62%).

Conclusion

Prophylactic anti-VEGF effectively prevents radiation maculopathy and is also beneficial in treating preexisting radiation maculopathy. Intensive treatment initially provides early benefits, but the efficacy diminishes after transitioning to a treat-and-extend regimen.

records.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.

content.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Current AI models for optical coherence tomography (OCT) primarily focus on diagnosis as a standalone task. We developed and validated an end-to-end agentic AI workflow that integrates automated macular hole (MH) diagnosis from OCT images with structured patient-friendly report generation.

Methods

The proposed sequential workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent consisted of an image diagnosis stage and a language generation step. The OCT version of RETFound, a self-supervised retinal foundation model, was fine-tuned for binary classification of macular OCT scans as MH or normal macula. Training, validation, and internal testing were performed using multiple public OCT datasets with patient-level stratified splitting, followed by external validation on two independent datasets. The performance of the fine-tuned foundation model was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC). For each new OCT image, the AI agent used the trained RETFound model to classify the image, received the diagnostic output, incorporated it into a structured prompt, and called the large language model (GPT-4) to generate the clinical report.

Results

On the internal test set (n = 180), the model achieved an accuracy of 100% (95% confidence interval (CI), 97.9-100%) with an AUC of 1.00. On external validation (n = 1014), accuracy was 98.8% (95% CI 97.9-99.3%), sensitivity was 97.9% (95% CI 96.3-98.8%), specificity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100.0%), and AUC was 0.999 (95% CI 0.998-1.000). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis showed that predictions were driven by relevant retinal regions, particularly the macular hole and adjacent layers. The end-to-end agentic AI workflow generated concise and standardized patient-friendly reports for all samples, without the language model influencing diagnostic decisions.

Conclusions

This study demonstrates the feasibility of an end-to-end AI workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent for robust OCT-based MH diagnosis with a large language model for structured report generation. By separating image-based diagnosis from language generation, this approach offers a practical and scalable solution for virtual vitreoretinal clinics.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology-in the form of Machine Learning (ML) models and other models specialized in image recognition and processing, such as Convolutional Neural Networks Visual Transformers (CNN-ViTs)-is increasingly being used in ophthalmology. This review summarizes the main AI applications for laser-assisted refractive surgery. Methods: A wide-ranging literature search on the PubMed and ISI Thompson Web of Science databases was conducted. Results: AI is an all-encompassing technological concept that refers to either specific applications of ML/CNN models, such as in keratoconus screening or diagnosis, or agentic/multimodal AI applications that process different data types using a variety of AI models. The most clinically established applications found were corneal ectasia and keratoconus screening, in which AI models can reliably exceed 95% diagnostic accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity; nomogram-derived laser ablation programming; optimization of ray-tracing calculations for ray-traced ablation profiles; patient screening and selection for refractive surgery; visual and refractive result prediction; assessment of postoperative corneal ectasia risk; detection of intraoperative complications; research on the laser coupling effect; and other applications such as monitoring eye rubbing behavior in corneal ectasia suspects. Thus, singular, specific applications of AI models have made the largest clinical contributions. These results must be interpreted with a comparison of internal versus external validation, calibration, and generalizability. Overall the technology is highly promising. Agentic/multimodal AI frameworks are currently being discussed, with pilot studies published and applicability proposed in the context of large, high-patient-volume clinical practices. The technological advent of SHAP force plot graphs and saliency maps has improved understanding of the factors that contribute mechanistically to AI model reasoning, leading to more informed clinical decisions or research applicability, such as in finding parameters or factors linked to postoperative ectasia. Conclusions: AI is already established in laser-assisted refractive surgery in the form of models specialized in data-intensive analysis. At present, the best-performing novel AI models originate from the domain of large or multi-hospital settings due to requirements for multiple latest-generation diagnostic devices, high-volume patient data, computing expertise, and resources. Future directions could include clinical standardization and trickle-down dissemination of the technology. Agentic/multimodal AI has the potential to benefit large clinical/patient settings or offer access to expert knowledge in smaller practice settings. Agentic/multimodal AI implementation is offset by challenges in complexity, the technological limitations of LLMs ("hallucinations"), and ethical and legislative factors.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Bioengineering: Innovations, Challenges, and Future Directions: A Narrative Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Bioengineering: Innovations, Challenges, and Future Directions: A Narrative Review.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming bioengineering, with applications ranging from diagnosis and biomedical imaging to wearable technologies, rehabilitation, biomaterials, biofabrication, and digital twins. This narrative review aims to examine the major innovations, challenges, and future directions of AI-enabled bioengineering, with particular attention to its clinical and translational development. The literature was searched in Scopus and PubMed, with emphasis on systematic reviews and meta-analyses and consideration of other relevant secondary literature across the main bioengineering domains. A total of 57 secondary publications were included in the principal evidence base. The review process was additionally informed by the ANDJ Narrative Review Checklist and an established qualification and scoring methodology applied to the selected secondary literature. The reviewed evidence shows a broad expansion of AI applications and increasing integration of intelligent technologies into bioengineering systems. However, important challenges remain, particularly regarding data quality and representativeness, validation and generalizability, reproducibility, safety, human oversight, ethical responsibility, equity, and regulatory requirements. Future developments are expected to increasingly involve multimodal, adaptive, connected, and human-centered systems integrating AI with sensing technologies, robotics, digital twins, and longitudinal data. Overall, AI-enabled bioengineering is progressing from promising technological applications toward increasingly integrated and translational systems. Its successful evolution will depend on combining technological innovation with robust clinical evidence, responsible development, and appropriate ethical and regulatory frameworks.

records.title: Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Exophthalmometry in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Multicenter, Multiethnic Validation Study.
records.publisher: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association

content.title: Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Exophthalmometry in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Multicenter, Multiethnic Validation Study.
content.abstract:
Background

Proptosis is the principal quantitative measure of disease severity in thyroid eye disease (TED), but Hertel exophthalmometry has substantial interobserver variability and requires in-person specialist visits. Existing deep learning (DL) proptosis-from-photograph models require studio-acquired images. We aimed to validate, in a multicenter multiethnic study, a DL model fine-tuned to estimate proptosis (mm) from nonstudio facial photographs-smartphone selfies or clinician-taken photographs.

Methods

This validation study included 361 patients with confirmed or suspected TED at three institutions. Data were collected prospectively at two Korean sites-Severance Hospital (SH; 203 patients/3654 facial images; internal validation) and Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH; 79/933; same-ethnicity external validation)-and retrospectively, from routine-care images, at one Spanish site, Virgen Macarena University Hospital (HUVM; 79/336; different-ethnicity external validation). Korean patients self-acquired selfies on six smartphone models per site using a capture-guidance application; Spanish images were clinician-acquired during routine care without such guidance. The model-a dual-stream ResNet-18 jointly processing a facial image and a per-pixel depth map (ZoeDepth)-outputs a proptosis estimate (mm) per eye from one photograph and was fine-tuned, from a previously published model trained on studio digital single-lens reflex photographs, for these nonstudio acquisitions. Hertel measurements by oculoplastic specialists served as the reference standard.

Results

On single-image analysis, the mean absolute error (MAE) versus Hertel measurement was 1.14 mm (Pearson correlation coefficient [PCC] 0.83) in SH, 1.44 mm (PCC 0.85) in SNUBH, and 1.58 mm (PCC 0.77) in HUVM, with predictions within 2 mm of Hertel in 83.6%, 71.3%, and 69.7% of images, respectively. Performance was consistent across 12 smartphone models (per-device MAE 1.11-1.54 mm). For detecting severe proptosis (Hertel ≥21 mm), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.94 (confidence interval 0.93-0.96), 0.91 (0.89-0.92), and 0.86 (0.82-0.91) in SH, SNUBH, and HUVM, respectively. Bland-Altman analysis revealed underestimation at the upper extreme.

Conclusions

An artificial intelligence model fine-tuned for nonstudio facial photographs achieved Hertel-level agreement and reliable severity discrimination across 2 ethnicities and 12 smartphones, both for patient self-acquired smartphone selfies and for clinician-acquired routine clinic photographs, providing a scalable approach for patient-facing and clinic-based monitoring of TED severity, pending further longitudinal validation.

records.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.

content.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.
content.abstract:
Aims

Whether a retinal artificial intelligence (AI) risk score reclassifies SCORE2 cardiovascular risk stratification in statin-naive adults across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary is uncertain. We evaluated the retinal AI risk score for 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prediction.

Methods

In 40,672 statin-naive UK Biobank participants (aged 40-69, without diabetes), cardiovascular risk categories and treatment recommendation status (Class I or IIa vs neither) were defined using the 2025 ESC/EAS focused-update framework. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusted for SCORE2 or for established risk factors. The incremental predictive value of adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation.

Results

Over a 10.0-year median follow-up (914 ASCVD events), the very high retinal AI risk group independently predicted ASCVD (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.32 vs low risk; p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 reclassified risk across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary (statin-eligibility NRI [net reclassification improvement] 0.012, p<0.001); reclassification was statistically significant but modest (continuous NRI 0.445, p<0.001), without C-index or net-benefit gain. In the statin-indicated subgroup, retinal AI risk groups further stratified risk (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.16; p<0.001). Statin-not-indicated participants in the high or very high retinal AI risk groups had numerically similar observed 10-year risk to all statin-indicated, untreated participants (p=0.758). There was no evidence of effect modification by clinically detectable retinal disorder (interaction p=0.93). Incremental value was greater in women than men (sex interaction p<0.001).

Conclusion

Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 produced modest bidirectional risk reclassification across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary; these findings warrant prospective validation.Abstract word count: 250 words.

records.title: Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Imaging Reporting: Practical Guidelines for Sonographers-A Narrative Review.

content.title: Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Imaging Reporting: Practical Guidelines for Sonographers-A Narrative Review.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering diagnostic ultrasound, supporting image acquisition, automated measurement, computer-aided diagnosis, and report drafting. Sonographers are primary users of these tools, yet sonographer-oriented guidance on their responsible use in imaging reporting remains fragmented. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence, reporting guidelines, trustworthiness frameworks, regulations, and professional standards relevant to AI-assisted imaging reporting to distill practical guidance for sonographers. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched, together with professional-body and regulatory documents published up to July 2026. The review maps AI applications across the reporting chain, from real-time acquisition guidance (AI-guided echocardiography achieving diagnostic-quality images in 98.8% of novice-obtained scans) to computer-aided diagnosis improving breast lesion assessment (area under the curve increasing from 0.83 to 0.87) and large language models drafting structured reports. Evidence on automation bias, deskilling, hallucinated content, algorithmic bias, and medico-legal accountability is critically appraised. Building on FUTURE-AI, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, and World Health Organization guidance, a phase-based good-practice framework is proposed, covering pre-use appraisal and training, verification during use, and documentation and audit after use. AI should augment, not replace, sonographer judgment; human oversight, verification of every AI output, transparent documentation, and continuing AI literacy are prerequisites for safe adoption in imaging reporting.

records.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.

content.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.
content.abstract:
Rationale and objectives

To evaluate the feasibility of a quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-structured reporting pipeline that integrates quantitative MRI software with large language models (LLMs) for structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers and generating clinician-facing report conclusions.

Materials and methods

A total of 192 patients with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI images from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database were randomly selected. A deep-learning model generated structured report findings based on nine indices related to brain atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space abnormalities, and compared with neuroradiologist-generated reference reports. Four LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3, and Llama 3.1 8B) generated clinician-facing conclusions from the structured findings. Generated conclusions were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale across four metrics (accuracy, relevance, clarity, and satisfaction). Output errors were assessed across four categories: language, omission, addition, and numeric errors.

Results

Structured report findings demonstrated high accuracy for CSF space analysis (77.6%-97.9%). Performance for ordinal visual scales was lower under strict matching (27.1%-57.8%) but improved with a one-grade tolerance (91.7%-97.4%). Among LLMs, GPT achieved the highest scores across most metrics (median score 5) and exhibited the lowest output error rates. Smaller models (Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B) showed overall lower performance, with more language, omission, and addition errors. MedGemma demonstrated intermediate performance, but the highest rate of numeric errors.

Conclusion

Our quantitative MRI-to-structured reporting pipeline, integrating quantitative MRI software with LLM-based conclusion generation, might be feasible for automated structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers.

records.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer.
records.publisher: Journal of clinical practice and research

content.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer.
content.abstract:
Objective

Prostate cancer, one of the most common cancers affecting men's health worldwide, ranks second among cancer-related deaths. Therefore, it represents a critical health issue, and early diagnosis is crucial. Several imaging and analytical methods are used to diagnose this condition.

Materials and methods

This study focuses on research conducted between 2021 and 2025 that analyzes, diagnoses, and grades prostate cancer based on histopathological images using machine learning and deep learning algorithms. In this context, the reviewed studies also include an analysis of findings related to preprocessing and feature extraction methods that may aid in prostate cancer detection, as well as the classifiers used.

Results

According to the findings of the reviewed studies, artificial intelligence-supported prostate cancer detection systems demonstrate high clinical performance and significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy of pathologists by enabling rapid diagnosis. The presented research findings indicate a need for comprehensive studies focusing on prostate cancer using histopathological images.

Conclusion

The integration of artificial intelligence is transforming prostate cancer pathology from a traditional and subjective process into a data-driven and standardized framework. This systematic analysis of histopathological images will make significant contributions to future prostate cancer research, help achieve more reliable results in clinical decision-making processes, and lay the groundwork for personalized medicine.

records.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.

content.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been significantly improved through deep learning techniques; however, the lack of interpretability remains a major challenge for clinical adoption. Methods: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-driven framework for multiclass brain tumor classification using a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) and four transfer learning models, namely ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNetB0. The models were trained and evaluated on a publicly available brain MRI dataset consisting of glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumor classes. Their classification performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), and confusion matrix analysis. To enhance transparency and interpretability, Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP were used to visualize and quantify the regions contributing to the classification decisions. Results: Experimental results state that the transfer learning models consistently outperformed the CNN by learning more discriminative feature representations while producing more localized and interpretable explanations. The agreement among Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP confirms that the proposed models predominantly relied on tumor regions rather than irrelevant background information, thereby improving the interpretability and reliability of the diagnostic predictions. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides an effective and explainable computer-aided diagnosis system that supports trustworthy deep learning-based brain tumor classification and has the potential for decision-making.

records.title: Artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and generative models for osteoporosis and bone disease prediction: a systematic review and future research roadmap.

content.title: Artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and generative models for osteoporosis and bone disease prediction: a systematic review and future research roadmap.
content.abstract: Osteoporosis is a major global health burden, with considerable morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new avenues for osteoporosis screening, bone mineral density quantification, fracture-risk prediction, and clinical decision support, but progress remains fragmented across machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), generative models, and multimodal learning. This systematic review brings these strands together and identifies priority research needs for AI-based osteoporosis prediction. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, studies were identified from Scopus and Google Scholar, published between January 2020 and the final search date of 30 June 2026, with two reviewers screening independently and resolving disagreements by consensus. Design-related risk-of-bias indicators, such as retrospective vs. prospective design, validation strategy, and reference standard, were recorded for every study; a full PROBAST, QUADAS-2, and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal is planned but not yet complete. Fifty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively and descriptively, without formal meta-analysis, given substantial heterogeneity. Findings spanned five themes: classical machine learning, deep learning for imaging, explainable AI, generative models, and multimodal learning. Deep learning achieved strong predictive accuracy (AUC 0.82-0.96), XAI improved clinical interpretability, generative models helped offset data scarcity, and multimodal approaches boosted performance by combining imaging and clinical data. Key gaps remain, including limited external validation, heavy reliance on retrospective data, poor generalisability, and limited regulatory readiness. Building on these findings, this review proposes MXGNet, a multimodal, explainable, generative framework incorporating privacy-preserving federated learning, intended to guide development of robust, interpretable, clinically deployable AI tools for osteoporosis prediction.

records.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.

content.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.
content.abstract:
Background

Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests.

Methods

A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation.

Results

For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54-0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37-0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33-0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss' κ 0.58). Class-specific interpretation performance varied by category; sensitivity was highest for normal pattern and restrictive defects (0.72), whereas sensitivity for obstructive defects was 0.27. F1-scores were highest for normal and restrictive defects (0.81 and 0.62, respectively).

Conclusion

The current findings suggest that ChatGPT 5.5 has a limited capability, at its current stage of development, to serve as a reliable tool for independent spirometry interpretation in clinical practice. Nevertheless, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical decision-making and educational tools. Prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm these findings.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects over 366 million adults and 139 million children worldwide, yet diagnosis remains fundamentally subjective, relying on clinical interviews, behavioral observations, and rating scales that yield inconsistent results across practitioners and settings. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) offer a paradigm shift toward objective, data-driven diagnosis by detecting complex patterns across neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and digital biomarkers that elude conventional assessment. Although AI-based ADHD research has grown exponentially, no comprehensive synthesis examines the full spectrum of data modalities, validation practices, and clinical translation readiness. This gap limits our understanding of which approaches are most promising for real-world implementation.

Objective

This scoping review will visually map the current evidence on AI-based ADHD classification with respect to predictive accuracy, data forms, data features, generalizability, and interpretability of models.

Methods

This scoping review will use the Joanna Briggs Institute approach to scoping reviews and follow the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five electronic databases (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and ACM Digital Library) will be systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Empirical studies in English involving the use of AI, ML, DL, or explainable AI to diagnose ADHD with a total sample size greater than 100 participants (ADHD and control groups combined) and a non-ADHD control group (individuals with typical development or healthy individuals) will be included. Two independent reviewers will screen the titles, abstracts, and full texts, and any conflicts will be resolved through either discussion or arbitration. A standardized Microsoft Excel template will be used to extract data that will include the following: bibliographic data, data modalities, data models, data validation approaches, performance metrics, and explainability approaches. Thematic and narrative analysis will be used to synthesize findings on 4 research questions that will address model performance, data modality contributions, data characteristics, and interpretability methods.

Results

The scoping review began in December 2025. Analysis and screening are in progress, with the scoping review expected to be completed and submitted for publication in June 2026.

Conclusions

This scoping review will provide the first comprehensive synthesis of AI-, ML-, and DL-based ADHD diagnostic classification studies, mapping the evidence across data modalities, validation practices, interpretability methods, and clinical translation readiness. Findings will inform future methodological standards and support the translation of AI-based diagnostic tools into clinical practice.

records.title: From algorithm performance to clinical value in AI-assisted skin cancer diagnostics.

content.title: From algorithm performance to clinical value in AI-assisted skin cancer diagnostics.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized.

Methods

We conducted a PRISMA-ScR-guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes.

Results

Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes.

Discussion

Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems.

Conclusion

Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.

records.title: Interpretable deep learning maps spatial morphological phenotypes to HCC and LUAD survival.

content.title: Interpretable deep learning maps spatial morphological phenotypes to HCC and LUAD survival.
content.abstract: The clinical adoption of deep learning in pathology is largely hindered by the "black box" nature of current models, which often obscure the biological basis of prognosis. Here, we introduce MorphX, an interpretable framework that predicts patient survival by explicitly decoding multi-scale morphological patterns from whole-slide images. Unlike conventional methods relying on latent features, MorphX fuses macro-scale tissue texture with micro-scale nuclear metrics to attribute risk to interpretable biological phenotypes. In a multi-center study spanning 1,067 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), MorphX achieves concordance indices of 0.775-0.799 in discovery cohorts. Crucially, we derive eight distinct morphology-based biomarkers-driven by texture heterogeneity in necrotic regions, lymphocyte density, and nuclear shape-that demonstrate reproducible survival associations across independent cohorts, offering a granular resolution of tumor aggressiveness that transcends traditional histological grading. By translating opaque computational predictions into validated biological insights, MorphX supports trustworthy, transparent, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven precision oncology.

records.title: The Influence of Large Language Model-Generated Artificial Intelligence Risk Estimates on Clinical Decision-Making in Breast Imaging: A Simulation-Based Study.

content.title: The Influence of Large Language Model-Generated Artificial Intelligence Risk Estimates on Clinical Decision-Making in Breast Imaging: A Simulation-Based Study.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools in radiology, yet their influence on clinical decision-making remains a significant concern. This study evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI)-generated malignancy risk estimates influence clinical decisions in breast imaging and assesses automation bias (AB) among radiology residents at different training levels. Methods: In this simulation-based study, 20 residents reviewed radiology reports for 15 synthetic breast imaging cases generated by ChatGPT-4 Turbo, each presented in either a concordant or discordant format. Participants were stratified into two groups based on their completion of a breast imaging rotation and evaluated each case by assigning a BI-RADS score, recommending management, and rating their confidence in the AI risk estimate. Diagnostic accuracy and independent predictors of AB were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) to account for reader-level clustering. Results: Overall management accuracy was significantly lower in cases with discordant AI outputs (p = 0.008). A similar, albeit non-significant, decreasing trend was observed for BI-RADS accuracy. While advanced residents maintained high management accuracy regardless of AI concordance, early-stage residents showed a sharp decline in discordant cases (77.3% vs. 45.3%; p = 0.006). This decline was most critical in malignant cases for early-stage residents, where accuracy dropped from 92.0% to 48.0% (p < 0.001). In the multivariable GEE logistic regression model, training level was the only independent predictor of AB (OR: 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03-0.28, p < 0.001). Conclusions: In this simulation study, advanced clinical training was associated with lower susceptibility to AB in breast imaging, although training level alone is unlikely to be a sufficient safeguard. Safe integration of AI tools will require caution among junior trainees alongside system-level measures such as model transparency and institutional oversight.

records.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract: The rapid accumulation of multi-omics data provides increasing opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, but the heterogeneity and high dimensionality of these datasets remain major challenges for data integration and analysis. This review examines the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence for multi-omics integration in cancer biomarker research. Common multi-omics data paradigms and integration strategies are discussed, followed by a review of the bioinformatics, machine learning and deep learning approaches applied across 84 included studies. Cross-study comparison showed limited recurrence among the reported biomarkers, with only 15 biomarkers identified in at least four studies. Further assessment of the 13 recurrent protein-coding biomarkers showed significant protein-protein interaction enrichment and functional convergence in cancer-related processes, particularly PI3K/AKT and ERBB2-related signaling. This review also highlights current challenges, including missing data, heterogeneity across datasets, limited independent validation and the interpretability of artificial intelligence models. Future research may benefit from integrating multi-omics data with clinical information, pathological imaging, electronic health records, single-cell multi-omics and radiomics, together with broader datasets and greater use of independent validation to support the translation of multi-omics biomarker findings into clinical applications.

records.title: Comparative analysis and optimization of multi-model artificial intelligence for microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections.
records.publisher: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

content.title: Comparative analysis and optimization of multi-model artificial intelligence for microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections.
content.abstract:
Background

Superficial fungal infections present a growing threat to global public health. Traditional diagnostic techniques, including microscopy and culture, are time-consuming and subjective, often limiting diagnostic accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic tools offer a promising adjunct to improve efficiency and standardization of microscopic fungal detection.

Methods

We systematically compared six deep learning models, including the You Only Look Once (YOLO) series, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) series and the Detection Transformer (DETR). Three evaluation datasets were constructed. Datasets 1 and 2 (derived from 4000 hyphae and 4500 spore images) were used to assess image-level detection using sensitivity, precision and F1 score. Dataset 1 was manually annotated for the YOLO series and DETR; Dataset 2 (unannotated) served as the CNN series' benchmark. Dataset 3 (1, 870 specimens from 1, 730 patients) was used to evaluate sample-level performance via confusion matrix analysis for the YOLO series and DETR models, employing medical records as the reference standard. The best-performing model was optimized and deployed into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform for real-time clinical decision support.

Results

YOLOv11 outperformed all other evaluated architectures. Detection was generally better at 400× than at 200× magnification. Notably, the F1 score for hyphae detection by YOLOv11 increased from 90.42% (200×) to 92.06% (400×). All models achieved higher accuracy for spores than hyphae. Patient-level confusion-matrix analysis confirmed YOLOv11 superiority. After optimizing an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.25 and the maximum confidence (Cmax) strategy, 200× hyphae F1 rose to 97.84% and the positive predictive value (PPV) to 98.27%. Subgroup analysis showed robust performance across different diseases, with tinea capitis reaching the highest F1 score (98.53%).

Conclusion

The optimized YOLOv11 model demonstrates potential as a rapid and standardized supportive tool for the microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections. Integration into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform demonstrates the feasibility of real-time AI-assisted fungal detection, offering a standardized tool to support clinical decision-making. This work supports AI as a potential complement to clinical and laboratory expertise, pending further validation in prospective and multi-center settings, and highlights its potential to streamline fungal infection diagnostic workflows.

records.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.

content.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Scoring System and Exploratory Multiomics in Ankylosing Spondylitis: Hip Severity and Age-at-Severe-Hip-Involvement Stratification.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Scoring System and Exploratory Multiomics in Ankylosing Spondylitis: Hip Severity and Age-at-Severe-Hip-Involvement Stratification.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Accurate diagnosis and assessment of hip involvement are important for the clinical management of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). This study aimed to develop and internally validate an artificial intelligence-based Ensemble Scoring System (ESS) for AS diagnosis and hip-disease severity assessment and to explore its association with heterogeneous immune-cell infiltration and age at first documented severe hip involvement.

Methods

A total of 5721 patients with pelvic radiographs and linked clinical records were retrospectively included. Participants were divided into training and held-out validation cohorts at a 7:3 ratio strictly at the patient level, with no patient or image overlap. Deep-learning features extracted by a convolutional neural network were integrated with clinical variables using XGBoost to construct task-specific ensemble deep-learning (EDL) models. Exploratory proteomic, transcriptomic, single-cell RNA-sequencing, immunohistochemical, and peripheral-blood analyses were performed to investigate AS-related immune infiltration. An exploratory immune ensemble (IE) score was constructed using the monocyte proportion and EDL score. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to examine the association between the IE score and age at severe hip involvement.

Results

The EDL model achieved AUCs of 0.978 for distinguishing AS from non-AS, 0.990 for identifying hip arthropathy among patients with AS, and 0.996 for identifying BASRI-Hip grade ≥ 3 among patients with hip arthropathy. Monocyte percentage was an influential feature across the three EDL classification tasks. Exploratory multiomics and immunohistochemical analyses showed higher LYN expression in AS than in the corresponding non-AS fracture-control groups and suggested that LYN expression was concentrated predominantly in monocytes. A high IE score was associated with earlier severe hip involvement, with estimated median ages at first documented severe hip involvement of 36 and 50 years in the high- and low-IE-score groups, respectively. This finding represents exploratory risk stratification and does not establish independent prediction of biological disease progression.

Conclusions

The ESS showed strong internal validation performance for AS diagnosis and hip-disease severity classification. Exploratory analyses linked LYN dysregulation in monocytes with heterogeneous immune infiltration, while the IE score was associated with earlier severe hip involvement. Prospective multicenter external validation is required before clinical application.

records.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve electrocardiographic detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), but available studies address distinct diagnostic questions. We systematically reviewed studies evaluating AI-based STEMI detection from 12-lead electrocardiograms and separately synthesized AI performance against a clinical reference standard, AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, and AI agreement with physician electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from January 2010 through March 10, 2025. Bivariate random-effects models generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (AUC). Twenty-six studies comprising 539,876 ECGs were included. In 20 studies comparing AI with a clinical reference standard, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.91-0.97), specificity 0.95 (0.90-0.98), AUC 0.98 (0.97-0.99), positive likelihood ratio 19.2 (9.3-39.5), and negative likelihood ratio 0.05 (0.03-0.10). In 8 studies reporting both AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, separate syntheses showed sensitivity of 0.91 (0.86-0.94) for AI versus 0.78 (0.69-0.85) for clinicians, specificity of 0.91 (0.82-0.96) for both, and AUCs of 0.95 and 0.90, respectively. In 7 studies using physician ECG interpretation as the comparator, AI sensitivity was 0.85 (0.70-0.94), specificity 0.99 (0.96-1.00), and AUC 0.98 (0.96-0.99). Sensitivity analyses excluding case-control designs, influential studies, and restricting analyses to deep learning models or raw waveform ECGs produced similar findings.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in the Management of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Narrative Review Informed by a Systematic Search.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in the Management of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Narrative Review Informed by a Systematic Search.
content.abstract:
Background

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of mortality, and early identification of phenotypes, exacerbation risk, and treatment response remains challenging. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool for improving prediction, classification, and monitoring in COPD. This narrative review, informed by a systematic search, evaluated current AI applications in COPD management.

Methods

The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024502765) and reported with reference to PRISMA 2020 principles. MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to May 2025. Eligible studies applied Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, or Deep Learning approaches to adult COPD populations for diagnostic, prognostic, monitoring, phenotyping, or disease management purposes. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and methodological quality was appraised using design-appropriate tools.

Results

Twenty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. AI demonstrated high discriminative accuracy for COPD diagnosis, exacerbation prediction, and mortality risk (mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve [AUROC] = 0.83), although methodological heterogeneity and limited external validation were common. Models integrating multimodal data generally outperformed single-domain approaches. Risk-of-bias assessment identified concerns related to small sample sizes, limited external validation, and incomplete reporting of model development and validation procedures.

Conclusion

Current evidence suggests that AI may support COPD diagnosis, prognostic prediction, and telemonitoring. However, methodological heterogeneity, limited external validation, and inconsistent reporting standards continue to limit clinical translation. Further high-quality, externally validated studies are needed to support implementation in respiratory care.

records.title: Multimodal Carotid Ultrasound-based Artificial Intelligence Model for Predicting Acute Ischemic Stroke Risk in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

content.title: Multimodal Carotid Ultrasound-based Artificial Intelligence Model for Predicting Acute Ischemic Stroke Risk in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
content.abstract:
Rationale and objectives

Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are at high risk of acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet accurate risk stratification remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and validate a multimodal model based on carotid ultrasound for improved AIS risk prediction.

Materials and methods

In this multicenter retrospective study, a total of 480 patients with T2DM who underwent carotid ultrasound were recruited from two centers, with one center (n=394) used for model development and the other (n = 86) for independent external testing. A dual-scale deep learning framework based on a Swin Transformer was developed to capture both local plaque features and surrounding vascular context. Deep learning features were integrated with radiomic and clinical features to construct a multimodal model. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), along with calibration and decision curve analysis.

Results

The multimodal model achieved AUCs of 0.952 (95% CI: 0.910-0.984) in the internal cohort and 0.939 (95% CI: 0.838-0.996) in the external cohort, showing improved performance compared to single-modality models. In the reader study, AI-assisted interpretation improved diagnostic performance across all readers, with AUC increases ranging from 0.760 to 0.857 and from 0.868 to 0.929 for senior readers, and from 0.450 to 0.700 and from 0.548 to 0.659 for junior readers. Generalized estimating equation analyses showed significant improvements in diagnostic correctness among both senior and junior readers, with P values of 0.00235 and 0.000343, respectively.

Conclusion

A multimodal framework integrating carotid ultrasound with clinical, radiomic, and deep learning features enables improved AIS risk stratification in patients with T2DM.

records.title: The application progress of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease.

content.title: The application progress of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease.
content.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, where traditional diagnostic methods are constrained by limited sensitivity and restricted clinical utility. This review synthesizes recent applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in AD diagnostics, focusing on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) across neuroimaging modalities and multi-omics research. AI algorithms can automatically extract subtle microstructural, metabolic, and molecular features, enabling high-precision classification of AD stages, patient stratification, and non-invasive early screening through multimodal data integration. However, translating AI into routine clinical practice still faces critical challenges, including high equipment costs, insufficient model generalizability across real-world cohorts, data class imbalance, and complex cross-platform standardization barriers. Future research should prioritize cost-effective surrogate modeling, robust multi-center validation, dynamic longitudinal integration, and mechanistic interpretability to accelerate the standardized clinical translation of AI-driven AD diagnostics.

records.title: Impact of motor guided imagery therapy on stroke patients with pain symptoms: a three-level meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Impact of motor guided imagery therapy on stroke patients with pain symptoms: a three-level meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Post-stroke pain is a common and intractable complication that hinders neurorehabilitation progress. Motor Guided Imagery (MGI), an emerging rehabilitation technique based on brain-computer interaction principles, has shown potential in relieving post-stroke pain, yet high-quality evidence on its multi-dimensional efficacy remains insufficient. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of MGI on pain, sensorimotor function, sleep quality, life status, and psychological mood in stroke patients using a three-level meta-analysis.

Objective

This study aimed to quantitatively assess the therapeutic effects of Motor Guided Imagery for stroke-related pain and explore potential intervention moderators using a three-level meta-analysis framework.

Methods

Eight Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to June 29, 2025, to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of MGI for stroke patients with pain. A three-level random-effects model was adopted to pool Hedges' g effect sizes, accompanied by heterogeneity testing, moderator analysis, influence analysis, and publication bias assessment. Influence-based outlier detection was implemented; analyses retaining all effect-size observations were treated as the primary main analysis, while outlier-removed analyses were reported only as supplementary sensitivity checks.

Results

Motor-guided imagery training significantly relieved pain (g = -0.524, 95% CI -0.779 to -0.269, p = 0.0006; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) and improved sleep quality (g = -1.658, 95% CI -2.115 to -1.201, p < 0.001; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) in stroke patients. Meanwhile, it significantly enhanced motor function (g = 1.395, 95% CI 0.963 to 1.826, p < 0.001), life status (g = 1.757, 95% CI 0.966 to 2.549, p = 0.0012), and psychological-emotional status (g = 1.729, 95% CI 1.045 to 2.413, p = 0.0002); positive Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for the latter three outcomes. Moderator analysis indicated that acute-phase intervention (≤4 weeks) and high-frequency regimens (>5 sessions/week) tended to produce better analgesic effects, while age, gender, single-session duration, and pain location had no significant moderating effects.

Conclusion

MGI may produce beneficial rehabilitation effects that can alleviate post-stroke pain and synergistically improve motor function, sleep, daily-living ability, and psychological state of stroke patients. Exploratory subgroup trends indicated potentially larger effects for early implementation within the acute phase and high-frequency short-duration regimens. However, these observations should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating clues given non-significant overall moderator tests. Further high-quality research is required to confirm these findings.

Registration

The systematic review protocol was retrospectively registered with PROSPERO under registration ID CRD420261278812, after literature search and full-text screening had been completed.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261278812; identifier: CRD420261278812.

records.title: Application of artificial intelligence in non-invasive cardiovascular imaging for coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Application of artificial intelligence in non-invasive cardiovascular imaging for coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a leading cause of death worldwide. While non-invasive imaging techniques are widely used for diagnosis, their interpretation can be time-consuming and subject to intra- and inter-observer variability. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, offers potential advantages in improving diagnostic accuracy and efficiency by rapidly processing large imaging datasets.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted to evaluate current evidence on AI applications in non-invasive CAD imaging. Searches were performed in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Engineering Index, and the Cochrane Library for studies published between 2018 and 2023. A total of 122 studies were included in the evidence map, and 9 studies assessing AI for detecting ≥50% coronary stenosis were selected for meta-analysis.

Results

The pooled sensitivity and specificity for detecting stenosis were 0.94 and 0.69, respectively, at the patient level, and 0.81 and 0.88 at the vessel level. The area under the SROC curve was 0.83 (patient level) and 0.92 (vessel level), indicating good diagnostic performance. High heterogeneity was observed across studies.

Discussion

These findings suggest that AI holds promise for enhancing the diagnostic process in CAD imaging. However, variability in methodologies and AI implementation underscores the need for standardization and further prospective validation.

records.title: Predicting Malignant Transformation in Oral Epithelial Dysplasia: A Systematic Comparison of Artificial Intelligence-Based Risk Models and Pathologist-Based Microscopy.
records.publisher: Journal of oral pathology & medicine : official publication of the International Association of Oral Pathologists and the American Academy of Oral Pathology

content.title: Predicting Malignant Transformation in Oral Epithelial Dysplasia: A Systematic Comparison of Artificial Intelligence-Based Risk Models and Pathologist-Based Microscopy.
content.abstract:
Background/aims

Risk prediction models (RPMs) based on histopathological analysis of oral epithelial dysplasia (OED) are increasingly used to stratify patients with oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and support personalized management. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)-based models compared with conventional human microscopy for predicting malignant transformation (MT).

Methods

A total of 32 studies published between 1998 and 2026 were included (9 AI-based and 23 human-based), focusing on OED in oral leukoplakia (OL), erythroleukoplakia, and erythroplakia. AI approaches addressed prediction or prognostic tasks using machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), or hybrid methods, with multilayer perceptron and random forest among the most frequently used algorithms.

Results

Meta-analysis demonstrated strong discriminative performance for AI models (pooled odds ratio [OR] = 12.64; 95% CI: 5.65-28.26; I2 = 57%). Human evaluation also confirmed a significant association between OED and MT (OR = 3.42; 95% CI: 2.07-5.68), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 85%). AI-based models showed higher specificity and more consistent performance, while sensitivity remained comparable to human assessment.

Conclusions

Overall, AI-based RPMs demonstrate promising and more reliable discriminative ability, primarily by improving decision precision rather than detection rates. However, further standardization, external validation, and larger multicentric datasets are required for clinical implementation.

records.title: Real-World Effectiveness of AI-Enabled Clinical Decision Support in Primary Care: Systematic Review.

content.title: Real-World Effectiveness of AI-Enabled Clinical Decision Support in Primary Care: Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

AI-enabled clinical decision support systems (CDSS) are being used in primary care, but their effects on clinical decisions and patient outcomes remain uncertain.

Objective

This study aimed to synthesize real-world evaluations of clinician-facing AI-enabled CDSS in primary care and assess evidence for diagnostic performance, changes in care, clinician efficiency, and patient-important outcomes.

Methods

Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020, 5 principal bibliographic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane CENTRAL, and CINAHL Ultimate), a supplementary EBSCOhost platform search, and 2 trial registries were searched for publications from 2011 through 2025. Eligible studies evaluated a learned (data-derived) or case-based AI component used by clinicians in routine primary or ambulatory care and reported a clinical, behavioral, process, efficiency, or diagnostic accuracy outcome. Screening was performed independently by 2 reviewers. Risk of bias was assessed with design-appropriate tools, and GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) was applied to 4 outcome bodies. Deterministic rule-based tools were retained only as contextual comparison.

Results

A total of 66 reports were assessed at full text, and 24 studies met the review criteria; 10 were AI-enabled and formed the appraised review population, while 14 deterministic studies were contextual only. Detection findings were inconsistent: AI electrocardiography increased new low ejection fraction diagnoses (odds ratio [OR] 1.32, 95% CI 1.01-1.61), whereas an electronic health record machine learning dementia marker used alone did not (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.63-1.11). Diagnostic studies showed high melanoma discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.960) but only moderate glaucoma discrimination (AUROC 0.80; sensitivity 65%). Nonrandomized before-after studies reported increased urinary tract infection treatment success (from 75% to 80%) and changed diabetic retinopathy screening criteria in 3 of 4 general practitioners. A pre-exposure prophylaxis trial was null overall; a multicomponent fall prevention CDSS improved shared decision-making, with inconclusive medication-change effects. Clinicians reported lower estimated record review time in asthma care. Neither trial assessing patient-important outcomes demonstrated benefit from AI-CDSS; one musculoskeletal functional outcome favored usual care.

Conclusions

Evidence published through December 2025 showed mixed effects of AI-enabled CDSS in primary care. Some studies reported improvements in detection or care processes, but patient-important benefit was not demonstrated. Heterogeneity and limited outcome measurement prevented causal explanations for these differences. Future trials should assess clinical decisions and patient outcomes together.

Trial registration

PROSPERO CRD420261302104; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261302104.

records.title: Advances in artificial intelligence for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis of neurological diseases: a systematic literature review.

content.title: Advances in artificial intelligence for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis of neurological diseases: a systematic literature review.
content.abstract: Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context. This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations. The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis. MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies. The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

records.title: Efficacy of platelet-rich plasma or plasma rich in growth factors in the treatment of thin endometrium: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Efficacy of platelet-rich plasma or plasma rich in growth factors in the treatment of thin endometrium: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Thin endometrium is a recognized cause of implantation failure in assisted reproduction, and conventional treatments are frequently disappointing. Intrauterine infusion of autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) or plasma rich in growth factors (PRGF) has emerged as a candidate therapy, but the randomized evidence remains limited and inconsistent.

Objective

To synthesize the randomized controlled evidence on the efficacy of intrauterine PRP or PRGF for women with thin endometrium, with clinical pregnancy as the primary outcome and biochemical pregnancy, endometrial thickness change, and cycle cancellation as secondary outcomes.

Design

Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

Methods

PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 30 April 2026. RCTs comparing intrauterine PRP or PRGF against a non-PRP control in women with thin endometrium were eligible. Risk of bias was appraised with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR) and endometrial thickness change as a mean difference (MD), using random-effects models with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Heterogeneity was quantified with the I-squared statistic, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed.

Results

Seven RCTs were included. For clinical pregnancy, five trials (343 participants) yielded a pooled RR of 2.32 (95% CI 1.02-5.31; p=0.047; I-squared=23.0%). PRP or PRGF significantly increased endometrial thickness (six trials, 370 participants; MD 0.94 mm, 95% CI 0.34-1.55; p=0.010) but with very high heterogeneity (I-squared=90.5%). Biochemical pregnancy (four trials, RR 2.32, 95% CI 0.71-7.52; p=0.108) and cycle cancellation (three trials, exploratory; RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.00-203.51; p=0.622) did not differ significantly. Leave-one-out analysis showed that the clinical-pregnancy result lost statistical significance when any of several trials was removed. Certainty of evidence was very low for pregnancy and thickness outcomes.

Conclusion

Intrauterine PRP or PRGF reliably increases endometrial thickness and shows a marginally significant, fragile improvement in clinical pregnancy, without demonstrable benefit for biochemical pregnancy or cycle cancellation. Given the small number of trials, high risk of bias, and very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be regarded as preliminary and require confirmation in larger, rigorously designed RCTs.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/home, identifier CRD420261383681.

records.title: A meta-analysis-informed diagnostic stratification tool for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome: systematic review, meta-analysis, and single-center cohort-based assessment.
records.publisher: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

content.title: A meta-analysis-informed diagnostic stratification tool for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome: systematic review, meta-analysis, and single-center cohort-based assessment.
content.abstract:
Background

This study aimed to develop and assess a meta-analysis-informed diagnostic stratification tool for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) in patients with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS).

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to identify bedside clinical factors associated with IPA/SFTS-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (SAPA) in patients with SFTS. Because individual participant data were unavailable, pooled study-level odds ratios were translated into a pragmatic three-variable diagnostic stratification score rather than a conventional individual-level prediction model. The tool was assessed in a separate single-center retrospective cohort of 220 patients with SFTS, among whom 63 (28.6%) met the clinically ascertained IPA/SAPA endpoint.

Results

Six studies involving 2,342 patients with SFTS, including 407 patients with IPA/SAPA, were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. In the primary random-effects analyses, neurological symptoms showed the clearest pooled association with increased IPA/SAPA risk, whereas ICU admission and corticosteroid use showed positive but less precise pooled directions of effect. The final three-variable score assigned 9 points for neurological symptoms, 9 points for ICU admission, and 6 points for corticosteroid use, yielding a total score range of 0-24 points. In the single-center cohort-based assessment, the diagnostic stratification tool showed encouraging discrimination, with an AUC of 0.910 (95% CI, 0.869-0.951) and a Brier score of 0.097 after cohort-based logistic recalibration. The observed IPA/SAPA incidence increased stepwise across low-, medium-, and high-risk groups: 3.7% (4/108), 22.8% (13/57), and 83.6% (46/55), respectively.

Conclusion

This meta-analysis-informed diagnostic stratification tool showed encouraging cohort-based risk separation in a single-center retrospective assessment. It may help prioritize fungal diagnostic work-up and surveillance intensity in patients with SFTS and support more targeted diagnostic resource allocation and antifungal stewardship. However, it should not be used as a stand-alone basis for antifungal treatment decisions or as a broadly generalizable individual-level prediction model. External validation, local recalibration, and prospective multicenter evaluation are required before clinical implementation.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=5115813, identifier CRD420251115813.

records.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Ophthalmology: Systematic Review.

content.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Ophthalmology: Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to revolutionize ophthalmic care, but their evaluation practice remains fragmented. A systematic assessment is crucial to identify gaps and guide future evaluation practices and clinical integration.

Objective

This study aims to map the current landscape of LLM evaluations in ophthalmology and explore whether performance synthesis is feasible for a common task.

Methods

A comprehensive search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore was conducted up to November 17, 2024 (no language limits). Eligible publications quantitatively assessed an existing or modified LLM on ophthalmology-related tasks. Studies without full-text availability or those focusing solely on vision-only models were excluded. Two reviewers screened studies and extracted data across 6 dimensions (evaluated LLM, data modality, ophthalmic subspecialty, medical task, evaluation dimension, and clinical alignment), and disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. Descriptive statistics were analyzed and visualized using Python (with NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, and Matplotlib libraries). The Fisher exact test compared open- versus closed-source models. An exploratory random-effects meta-analysis (logit transformation; DerSimonian-Laird τ2) was performed for the diagnosis-making task; heterogeneity was reported with I2 and subgrouped by model, modality, and subspecialty.

Results

Of the 817 identified records, 187 studies met the inclusion criteria. Closed-source LLMs dominated: 170 for ChatGPT, 58 for Gemini, and 32 for Copilot. Open-source LLMs appeared in only 25 (13.4%) of studies overall, but they appeared in 17 (77.3%) of evaluation-after-development studies, versus 8 (4.8%) pure-evaluation studies (P<1×10-5). Evaluations were chiefly text-only (n=168); image-text tasks, despite the centrality of imaging, were used in 19 studies. Subspecialty coverage was skewed toward comprehensive ophthalmology (n=72), retina and vitreous (n=32), and glaucoma (n=20). Refractive surgery, ocular pathology and oncology, and ophthalmic pharmacology each appeared in 3 or fewer studies. Medical query (n=86), standardized examination (n=41), and diagnosis making (n=29) emerged as the 3 predominant tasks, while research assistance (n=5), patient triaging (n=3), and disease prediction (n=3) received less attention. Accuracy was reported in most studies (n=176), whereas calibration and uncertainty were almost absent (n=5). Real-world patient data (n=45), human performance comparison (n=63), non‑English testing (n=24), and real-world deployment (n=4) were relatively absent. Exploratory meta-analysis pooled 28 diagnostic evaluations from 17 studies: overall accuracy was 0.594 (95% CI 0.488-0.692) with extreme heterogeneity (I2=94.5%). Subgroups remained heterogeneous (I2>80%), and findings were inconsistent (eg, pooled GPT-3.5>GPT-4).

Conclusions

Evidence on LLM evaluations in ophthalmology is extensive but heterogeneous. Most studies have tested a few closed-source LLMs on text-based questions, leaving open-source systems, multimodal tasks, non-English contexts, and real-world deployment underexamined. High methodological variability precludes meaningful performance aggregation, as illustrated by the heterogeneous meta-analysis. Standardized, multimodal benchmarks and phased clinical validation pipelines are urgently needed before LLMs can be safely integrated into eye care workflows.

records.title: Can we really trust generative models in healthcare? A systematic review of uncertainty quantification in generative AI for medical imaging.
records.publisher: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine

content.title: Can we really trust generative models in healthcare? A systematic review of uncertainty quantification in generative AI for medical imaging.
content.abstract:
Background and objective

Generative AI is transforming medical imaging research through synthesis, enhancement, and reconstruction of clinical images.
